content: Parental substance use, involving alcohol and illicit drugs (excluding tobacco), represents a significant public health and child welfare concern. Numerous interventions have been developed to address this issue, aiming to reduce substance misuse among parents and improve outcomes for both parents and their children. This review evaluates the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions in reducing parental substance use. The review included 22 studies with a total of 2,274 participants, whose average age ranged from 26.3 to 40.9 years. Most of the studies (73%) focused exclusively on mothers. The substances most commonly reported by participants were heroin, cocaine, and alcohol. The interventions were categorized into three types: those targeting parenting only (59%), those addressing substance use only (23%), and integrated interventions that combined both parenting and substance use components (27%). Half of the studies compared the experimental intervention to usual treatment, while others used minimal intervention, attention controls, or alternative interventions as comparators. Eight studies provided data on the primary outcome—reduction in the frequency of parental substance use—at sixand/or twelve-month follow-ups. These data were included in a meta-analysis. The quality of evidence was assessed as moderate for most outcomes, except for certain domains such as blinding of participants and personnel, which were at low or unclear risk of bias. The findings suggest that psychosocial interventions are likely effective in reducing the frequency of parental alcohol misuse. At six months, there was a moderate reduction in alcohol use (mean difference [MD] −0.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] −0.51 to −0.13; six studies, 475 participants). At twelve months, the reduction was slightly smaller but still significant (standardized mean difference [SMD] −0.25, 95% CI −0.47 to −0.03; four studies, 366 participants). For drug use, a significant reduction was observed only at twelve months (SMD −0.21, 95% CI −0.41 to −0.01; six studies, 514 participants). When examining the type of intervention, psychosocial interventions targeting substance use alone showed limited effectiveness. For alcohol misuse, the reduction was not significant at six months (SMD −0.35, 95% CI −0.86 to 0.16; two studies, 89 participants) or twelve months (SMD −0.09, 95% CI −0.86 to 0.61; one study, 34 participants). Similarly, for drug use, no significant reduction was observed at six months (SMD 0.01, 95% CI −0.42 to 0.44; two studies, 87 participants) or twelve months (SMD −0.08, 95% CI −0.81 to 0.65; one study, 32 participants). Parenting-only interventions, without a substance use component, also showed limited effectiveness. For alcohol misuse, the reduction was not significant at six months (SMD −0.21, 95% CI −0.46 to 0.04; three studies, 273 participants) or twelve months (SMD −0.11, 95% CI −0.64 to 0.41; two studies, 219 participants). For drug use, no significant reduction was observed at six months (SMD 0.10, 95% CI −0.11 to 0.30; four studies, 407 participants) or twelve months (SMD −0.13, 95% CI −0.52 to 0.26; three studies, 351 participants). Integrated interventions, which combined parenting and substance use components, showed more promise. These interventions were associated with small but significant reductions in alcohol misuse at six months (SMD −0.56, 95% CI −0.96 to −0.16) and twelve months (SMD −0.42, 95% CI −0.82 to −0.03; two studies, 113 participants). Similarly, reductions in drug use were observed at six months (SMD −0.39, 95% CI −0.75 to −0.03) and twelve months (SMD −0.43, 95% CI −0.80 to −0.07; two studies, 131 participants). However, the quality of this evidence was low. Interventions involving children in the sessions were not effective in reducing parental alcohol or drug use. In contrast, interventions that excluded children from the sessions were associated with reductions in alcohol misuse at six months (SMD −0.47, 95% CI −0.76 to −0.18; three studies, 202 participants) and twelve months (SMD −0.34, 95% CI −0.69 to 0.00; two studies, 147 participants). A reduction in drug use was also observed at twelve months (SMD −0.34, 95% CI −0.69 to 0.01; two studies, 141 participants). However, the quality of this evidence was low. The effectiveness of interventions appeared to differ between mothers and fathers. For mothers, there was lowto very low-quality evidence of a reduction in alcohol misuse at six months only (SMD −0.27, 95% CI −0.50 to −0.04; four studies, 328 participants). For fathers, reductions in alcohol misuse were observed at six months (SMD −0.43, 95% CI −0.78 to −0.09; two studies, 147 participants) and twelve months (SMD −0.34, 95% CI −0.69 to 0.00; two studies, 147 participants). Reductions in drug use were also observed for fathers at six months (SMD −0.31, 95% CI −0.66 to 0.04; two studies, 141 participants) and twelve months (SMD −0.34, 95% CI −0.69 to 0.01; two studies, 141 participants). In conclusion, psychosocial interventions likely reduce the frequency of parental alcohol and drug use, with integrated interventions showing the most promise. However, mothers may benefit less than fathers, potentially due to the lack of substance use components in interventions targeting mothers. Interventions involving children do not appear to be effective. The overall quality of evidence ranged from low to moderate, and further research is needed to confirm these findings.
